name: Job Scheduler
tagline: From a crontab on one box to a sharded scheduler with leases, retries and priorities
summary: A job scheduler answers two deceptively simple questions: what is due right now, and who is going to run it. The first version is a crontab and takes one line. It becomes a distributed-systems problem the moment the box can reboot, the job can fail halfway, the run can take longer than its interval, or a second scheduler replica is added for availability and both replicas decide the same job is due. Each step below keeps the previous design and changes only what the new scale or requirement demands, and the two hardest ideas — at-least-once versus exactly-once execution, and what to do about clock skew and windows that were missed while nothing was running — are argued where they first bite.
requirements: Run recurring jobs from a cron expression and one-off jobs at a given timestamp, starting within an agreed tolerance (say 5 seconds at p99).
A job must never run twice concurrently, and a job that already succeeded must not be re-executed by a retry or a replay.
Failures are retried with exponential backoff up to a limit; anything past the limit lands somewhere an operator can see and replay.
No scheduled run is silently lost when a scheduler or worker crashes, deploys or is partitioned from the store.
The policy for windows missed while the system was down is explicit per job: skip, run once on recovery, or backfill every missed occurrence.
Urgent jobs are not starved by a flood of bulk jobs, and one slow job type cannot block unrelated ones.
Operators can see, for any job, its next run, its recent history with durations and errors, and current queue lag.

steps.title: Cron on a single box
steps.problem: Nothing has broken yet — this is the starting point. Some work simply must not happen inside a request: a nightly report, an hourly cache warm-up, a daily cleanup. The simplest correct answer is the operating system's own scheduler.
steps.why: Cron is already installed, already reliable and costs nothing to operate: a crontab line names a schedule and a command, and the OS forks the process at the right minute. For a handful of jobs on one machine there is no better answer, and reaching for a queue here would be pure overhead. The limits are worth naming now because every later step removes one of them. Cron has no memory: if the machine is rebooting at 03:00 the nightly job simply does not happen and nothing records that it did not. It has no concurrency control, so if a run takes 70 minutes and the schedule is hourly you get two overlapping copies corrupting each other's work. It has no retry, no history and no visibility beyond whatever the script writes to a log file. And because the schedule is evaluated against this machine's clock, a drifting clock silently shifts every job. We accept all of that here because the cost of anything better is not justified by one box.

nodes.label: Cron daemon
nodes.why: Evaluates crontab entries once a minute against the local clock and forks a process when one matches. No state is kept between minutes.

nodes.label: Job script
nodes.why: A plain script sharing the application's code and credentials. If it exits non-zero nothing retries it and nothing is alerted.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL
nodes.why: The data the job reads and writes. Note that two overlapping runs of the same job hit these tables at the same time with no coordination.

nodes.label: Log file
nodes.why: stdout and stderr redirected to disk. Answering 'did last night's job run' means grepping this file by hand.

steps.title: A durable job table with claim and lease
steps.scale: 2-3 app servers · hundreds of jobs · thousands of runs a day
steps.problem: Three things broke at once. The box rebooted during a deploy at 03:00 and the nightly billing export simply never happened — and nobody noticed for two days. A weekly job began taking longer than a week's gap on a busy dataset, so two copies ran together and double-counted rows. And when the team added a second app server for availability, both servers' crontabs fired the same job. The schedule and the run history have to become data, not a file on one machine.
steps.why: We move the schedule into the database as two tables: `jobs` holds the definition (cron expression, payload, timeout, retry policy, `next_run_at`) and `job_runs` holds one row per attempt (state, started_at, finished_at, error, attempt number). A lightweight ticker on every app server wakes every few seconds and claims work with a single atomic statement — `SELECT ... WHERE next_run_at <= now() AND state = 'ready' FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT n` — then marks the rows `running`, stamps a `lease_expires_at` a couple of minutes out and computes the next occurrence. `SKIP LOCKED` is what makes several tickers safe: each transaction takes different rows, so no two servers claim the same run without any explicit lock. The lease is what makes crashes safe: a runner heartbeats by pushing `lease_expires_at` forward while it works, and a sweeper returns any run whose lease has expired to `ready`, so a killed process loses at most one lease interval rather than the job. This is the point where you must accept a delivery guarantee: because the runner can die after doing the work but before committing `succeeded`, the sweeper will hand that run out again — the system is **at-least-once**, and job bodies must therefore be safe to repeat. Exactly-once is not available in general; what is available is at-least-once delivery plus idempotent effects, which step 4 makes explicit. Clock skew stops mattering for scheduling because `now()` is read from the database, not from each server, so all tickers agree on what is due; only the database's clock must be sane. Missed windows also become a policy rather than an accident: because `next_run_at` is persisted, a system that was down for three hours can see exactly which occurrences it missed, and each job declares whether to skip them, run once on recovery, or backfill them all. The cost is a poll against the database every few seconds per server and a schema that now needs migrations and cleanup of old run rows.

nodes.label: Scheduling API
nodes.why: Creating a job is now an API call that writes a row, so schedules are reviewable and no longer edited by hand on a server.

nodes.label: Ticker (every 5 s)
nodes.why: Runs on every app server. One atomic claiming statement per tick means adding servers adds throughput instead of duplicates.

nodes.label: jobs + job_runs
nodes.why: FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED gives race-free claiming, lease_expires_at gives crash recovery, and next_run_at makes missed windows visible instead of lost.

nodes.label: Runner
nodes.why: Heartbeats its lease while working, then commits the terminal state. Because it can die between the effect and the commit, execution is at-least-once.

nodes.label: Lease sweeper
nodes.why: Any run whose lease expired is returned to ready. This is what turns a crashed process into a delayed retry instead of a lost job.

nodes.label: Application data
nodes.why: Unchanged by the scheduler, but now protected from overlapping runs because a claimed run is exclusive for the length of its lease.

steps.title: Queue and worker pool with retries and a dead-letter queue
steps.problem: The runner became the bottleneck. Jobs executed inside the app servers, so a report that pinned a CPU for ten minutes made user requests slow, and one job type that hung on an external API held its lease and blocked the tick behind it. Retries were a manual re-run by an engineer reading the run table, backoff did not exist so a failing job hammered a broken downstream service every five seconds, and a job that could never succeed retried for ever with no one watching.
steps.why: Execution is separated from scheduling. The scheduler's only remaining job is to decide what is due and publish a small message — the `run_id` and nothing else — onto a broker; a pool of workers, deployed and scaled independently of the API, consumes it and does the work. The payload stays out of the message so the database remains the single source of truth and a redelivered message cannot carry stale arguments. A broker rather than direct hand-off buys three things: buffering, so a burst of due jobs queues instead of failing; independent scaling of workers per job type; and per-message acknowledgement with a visibility timeout, which is the broker's version of the lease. RabbitMQ is chosen over Kafka here because the access pattern is competing consumers on individual messages with per-message acks, delays and requeues — a work queue, not a replayable log; Kafka's partition-ordered log would make per-message retry and priority awkward, and step 5 revisits that when volume and priority tiers change the calculus. Retries move into policy: on failure the worker computes an exponential backoff with jitter (say 10 s, 40 s, 160 s, ±20%) and schedules the next attempt, so a broken downstream gets breathing room and a thousand simultaneous failures do not retry in lockstep. Jitter matters more than the base delay. After the attempt limit the run goes to a dead-letter queue with its error and full history, which converts 'retries for ever, unnoticed' into a visible queue with a size an alert can watch and an operator can replay. Distinct queues per job class also stop one slow type from starving the rest. The delivery guarantee has not improved — broker redelivery is still at-least-once, and now there are two sources of duplication (lease expiry and message redelivery) — so the pressure to make job bodies idempotent has gone up, which is exactly what the next step addresses. The costs: a broker to operate and monitor, a second failure mode (queue backlog) to alert on, and the loss of a single place to read the whole story of a run unless the run table stays authoritative.

nodes.label: Scheduling API
nodes.why: Unchanged, except it no longer shares a process with anything that executes work.

nodes.label: Scheduler
nodes.role: Decide what is due, enqueue it
nodes.why: Reduced to one responsibility: claim due runs and publish run ids. It is now small enough to reason about, which matters for step 4.

nodes.label: jobs + job_runs
nodes.why: Still holds schedules, attempt counts and history. Messages carry only a run id so a redelivery cannot resurrect an old payload.

nodes.label: RabbitMQ
nodes.why: Competing consumers, per-message ack with a visibility timeout, delayed redelivery for backoff. Separate queues keep a slow job class from blocking others.

nodes.label: Worker pool A
nodes.why: Scaled independently of the API, so a CPU-heavy report no longer competes with user requests.

nodes.label: Worker pool B
nodes.why: A separate pool and queue for a job class with different resource needs or a flaky dependency.

nodes.label: Retry policy
nodes.why: Turns a failure into a scheduled later attempt instead of an immediate hammering; jitter prevents a thousand failures retrying in lockstep.

nodes.label: Dead-letter queue
nodes.why: A bounded, alertable place for runs that cannot succeed, with the error and history attached so an operator can fix and replay rather than dig.

nodes.label: Application data
nodes.why: Now written by many workers concurrently, which is why per-job concurrency limits stay in the job definition.

steps.title: Distributed scheduler with leader election and idempotent execution
steps.scale: 3 scheduler replicas · 50 workers · multiple availability zones
steps.problem: The single scheduler was a single point of failure: when it crashed on a Friday evening nothing was enqueued until Monday. Running three replicas fixed availability and created a worse bug — all three found the same due row in the gap before the claim committed and enqueued it three times, so one customer received three invoice emails. Meanwhile the duplicates already implied by at-least-once delivery finally caused visible damage: a payment-capture job that was redelivered after a worker crash charged a card twice.
steps.why: Two independent problems, two separate mechanisms. First, exactly one replica may act as scheduler at a time, so the replicas elect a leader by holding a lease in a store that offers a compare-and-swap primitive and a TTL: the leader renews its lease every few seconds, and if it stops renewing — crash, pause, network partition — the lease expires and a standby takes over. The critical detail is that the leader must treat its own lease as authoritative and stop enqueuing as soon as renewal fails, because a garbage-collection pause can leave a process believing it is leader after another has taken over; combining the lease with the row-level claim from step 2 means even a brief two-leader window cannot enqueue the same run twice. Choosing a consensus-backed store (etcd, ZooKeeper, Consul) over a Redis lock matters here: a Redis lease is fast and simple but is not safe under failover, while a Raft-backed store gives a real linearizable compare-and-swap. Second, duplicates from redelivery are made harmless rather than impossible. Every enqueued message carries the `run_id` as an idempotency key; before doing anything with an external effect the worker inserts that key into an idempotency table inside the same transaction as the effect, or calls the downstream API with the key so the provider deduplicates. A duplicate delivery then finds the key present and returns the recorded result instead of charging the card again. This is the honest form of exactly-once: at-least-once delivery plus effects that are idempotent, which is achievable, rather than exactly-once delivery, which is not. Clock skew is contained by keeping all 'is it due' decisions against the store's clock and by making the tolerance window comfortably larger than the observed skew and the tick interval; a job whose window was missed because the leader was mid-failover follows the per-job missed-window policy — skip, run once, or backfill — rather than being lost or fired an unbounded number of times. The costs are a consensus store to run and understand, a failover gap of roughly one lease TTL during which nothing is enqueued (which the tolerance in the requirements must absorb), and idempotency keys threaded through every job that touches an external system.

nodes.label: Scheduling API
nodes.why: Stateless and replicated; it never decides what is due, so it needs no coordination.

nodes.label: Scheduler A (leader)
nodes.why: The only replica allowed to publish. It renews its lease continuously and stops enqueuing the instant a renewal fails.

nodes.label: Scheduler B (standby)
nodes.why: Idle but healthy. It acquires the lease when it expires, which bounds the outage to roughly one TTL instead of a weekend.

nodes.label: etcd (leader lease)
nodes.why: A consensus-backed lease is safe across failover in a way a plain Redis lock is not; that safety is the entire point of this component.

nodes.label: jobs + job_runs
nodes.why: Still claims rows atomically, which is the second line of defence if two processes ever believe they are leader at once.

nodes.label: RabbitMQ
nodes.why: Unchanged, and still at-least-once: messages may be redelivered after a worker crash, which is now expected rather than feared.

nodes.label: Worker pool
nodes.why: Uses run_id as an idempotency key, so a redelivered message reads the recorded outcome instead of repeating the effect.

nodes.label: Worker pool (bulk)
nodes.why: Same contract; separated so long bulk runs cannot occupy every consumer slot.

nodes.label: Idempotency store
nodes.why: Written in the same transaction as the effect where possible; this is what makes at-least-once delivery acceptable for payments and emails.

nodes.label: Application data
nodes.why: Effects land here; the idempotency key and the write share a transaction so a crash cannot leave one without the other.

steps.title: Sharded partitions, priority tiers and full observability
steps.scale: Millions of schedules · tens of thousands of runs per minute · multi-tenant
steps.problem: A single leader could no longer scan millions of schedules inside the five-second tolerance — the due query alone took longer than the tick, so jobs drifted minutes late and the p99 requirement was violated every day. A tenant importing ten million rows filled the shared queue with bulk work and urgent password-reset jobs sat behind it for twenty minutes. And when a customer asked why job X did not run at 09:00, nobody could answer: the run row said 'succeeded' but there was no way to see the queue lag, the retry that preceded it or the downstream call that timed out.
steps.why: The scheduler stops being one process and becomes a set of shards. Schedules are partitioned by a hash of the job id into a fixed number of partitions, and a control plane — the same lease store, now used for assignment rather than a single leader — assigns partitions to scheduler instances and reassigns them when one dies. Each instance only queries its own partitions, so due-scan cost per instance falls with the number of instances and the tolerance window is met again; the job store is partitioned on the same key with an index on (partition, next_run_at) so the due query touches a narrow, hot range instead of the whole table. Ownership per partition preserves the step-4 property that at most one process enqueues a given run, without one process having to own everything. Priority is solved by separating flows rather than by a priority field: distinct topics or queues per tier (urgent, standard, bulk) with their own worker pools and their own concurrency limits, plus a per-tenant quota so no single tenant can occupy an entire tier. This is bulkheading — the important guarantee is not that urgent work is faster but that bulk work cannot consume the capacity urgent work needs. At this volume a partitioned log becomes attractive for the high-throughput bulk tier because sequential appends and consumer-group rebalancing scale further than per-message acknowledgement, while the low-volume urgent tier keeps a classic broker for its per-message retry and delay semantics; running both is a real operational cost and only worth it once one tier's volume dwarfs the other. Finally, observability becomes part of the product rather than an add-on: every run carries a trace id from the API call or the tick that created it through the queue into the worker and out to its downstream calls, so 'why was this late' resolves into a timeline of enqueue lag, wait time, attempt history and downstream latency. Metrics that matter are scheduling delay (due time to enqueue), queue lag per tier, run duration percentiles per job type, and dead-letter depth; those become the SLOs, and alerts fire on delay and lag rather than on CPU. The costs are substantial: partition assignment is now a distributed protocol with its own bugs, rebalancing briefly pauses enqueuing for the moved partitions, two messaging systems and several worker pools must be operated, and trace and metric volume roughly tracks run volume so retention has to be deliberate.

nodes.label: Scheduling API
nodes.why: Validates cron expressions, enforces per-tenant quotas and tags every schedule with its tier and partition key.

nodes.label: Control plane
nodes.why: Uses the same lease store to own the assignment map and to reassign a dead shard's partitions, so ownership stays exclusive without one global leader.

nodes.label: Scheduler shard 0
nodes.why: Queries only the partitions it owns, which is what brings the due scan back inside the tolerance window.

nodes.label: Scheduler shard N
nodes.why: Horizontal scaling of scheduling itself: add shards, add due-scan throughput.

nodes.label: Partitioned job store
nodes.why: Indexed on (partition, next_run_at) so each shard reads a narrow hot range; old run history is rolled off by partition instead of by row-by-row deletes.

nodes.label: Urgent queue
nodes.why: Keeps per-message ack, delay and retry semantics where they are worth the overhead — password resets, MFA codes, payment captures.

nodes.label: Bulk log (Kafka)
nodes.why: Sequential appends and consumer groups scale past per-message acknowledgement; ordering per partition is acceptable for imports and exports.

nodes.label: Urgent workers
nodes.why: Its own pool with its own limits, so a flood of bulk work cannot take the capacity urgent runs depend on.

nodes.label: Bulk workers
nodes.why: Scales on queue lag; can be starved without breaking any latency promise, which is exactly why it is separate.

nodes.label: Idempotency store
nodes.why: Unchanged and now essential: with two messaging systems and rebalancing there are more ways for a run to be delivered twice.

nodes.label: Tracing + metrics
nodes.role: Trace from tick to downstream call
nodes.why: A trace id follows the run through queue and worker, so 'why was this late' becomes a timeline rather than a guess.

nodes.label: SLOs & alerts
nodes.why: Alerting on due-to-enqueue delay, lag per tier and dead-letter depth catches the failures users notice, unlike CPU alerts.

textAlternative: Five diagrams show a job scheduler growing. Step 1: a cron daemon forks a job script on one server, which reads and writes PostgreSQL and appends to a log file. Step 2: a scheduling API writes schedules into jobs and job_runs tables; tickers on each app server claim due rows atomically with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, a runner heartbeats a lease while executing, and a sweeper reclaims runs whose leases expired. Step 3: the scheduler only enqueues run ids onto RabbitMQ queues split by job class; independent worker pools consume them, a retry policy requeues failures with exponential backoff and jitter, and exhausted attempts land in a dead-letter queue. Step 4: three scheduler replicas elect a leader through an etcd lease so only one enqueues, and workers deduplicate redelivered messages against an idempotency store keyed by run id, making at-least-once delivery safe. Step 5: schedules are partitioned across scheduler shards assigned by a control plane, work is split into an urgent RabbitMQ queue and a bulk Kafka log with separate worker pools, and traces plus SLO alerts on scheduling delay and queue lag make lateness diagnosable.
